questions.title: The clavicle's subcutaneous course
questions.question: Considering the true anatomical fact about the clavicle is

options.A: The lateral end is somewhat quadrangular in shape
options.B: It is subcutaneous throughout its whole extent
options.D: It is a short bone that lies horizontally across the root of the neck

explanations.A: Incorrect. The clavicle's lateral (acromial) end is flattened, not quadrangular; a quadrangular cross-section describes its medial part instead.
explanations.B: Correct. The clavicle is the one long bone of the body that is subcutaneous throughout its whole extent, lying immediately deep to the skin with no overlying muscle anywhere along its S-shaped course from the sternal end medially to the acromial end laterally. This subcutaneous position is exactly why the clavicle can be palpated along its whole length in a living subject and is also why it is one of the most commonly fractured bones, since nothing cushions it from a fall onto the shoulder or an outstretched hand. Its superior surface is smooth, not rough, which rules out one of the alternative statements printed alongside this fact.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The clavicle's superior surface is smooth; it is the inferior surface that carries roughened areas for ligament attachment.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The clavicle is classified as a long bone, not a short bone, despite lying horizontally; its shaft is longer than it is wide, the defining feature of a long bone.

questions.subject: msk
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Musculoskeletal System > Upper Limb Bones
questions.learning_objective: State that the clavicle is subcutaneous throughout its whole extent, with no overlying muscle.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: It is subcutaneous throughout its whole extent" (QUIZ11&12 Q1).

questions.title: The scapular spine and the acromion
questions.question: The scapula is

options.A: The lateral end of the spine forms the acromion, which articulates with the clavicle
options.C: The anterior surface is divided by the spine into the supraspinous fossa above and an infraspinous fossa below
options.D: The medial angle of the scapula forms the pear-shaped glenoid cavity

explanations.A: Correct. The scapula's posterior surface carries a prominent spine dividing it into a supraspinous fossa above and an infraspinous fossa below. The spine's lateral end projects forward and flattens into the acromion, a subcutaneous process overhanging the shoulder joint that articulates with the lateral end of the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint. This acromion-clavicle articulation is the scapula's own direct bony link to the rest of the shoulder girdle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The coracoid process projects forward, not backward, from the scapula's superior border.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is the posterior surface, not the anterior surface, that the spine divides into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae; the scapula's anterior (costal) surface is a single shallow concavity, the subscapular fossa.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the lateral angle of the scapula, not the medial angle, that carries the pear-shaped glenoid cavity receiving the humeral head.

questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Musculoskeletal System > Upper Limb Bones
questions.learning_objective: State that the lateral end of the scapular spine forms the acromion, which articulates with the clavicle.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The lateral end of the spine forms the acromion, which articulates with the clavicle" (QUIZ11&12 Q2).

questions.title: The humerus below its head
questions.question: The correct statement about the humerus is

options.A: The humerus articulates only with the scapula at the shoulder joint
options.B: On the medial aspect of the shaft is a roughened elevation called the deltoid tuberosity
options.C: The lower end of the humerus consists of the medial and lateral epicondyles only
options.D: Immediately below the head is the surgical neck. Below the neck are the greater and lesser tuberosities, separated from each other by the bicipital groove

explanations.A: Incorrect. The humerus articulates with the scapula at the shoulder joint and also with the radius and ulna at the elbow joint; it does not articulate only with the scapula.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The deltoid tuberosity lies on the lateral, not medial, aspect of the humeral shaft.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The humerus's lower end carries more than just the two epicondyles; it also carries the capitulum and trochlea, the articular surfaces that meet the radius and ulna at the elbow.
explanations.D: Correct. Immediately below the rounded head of the humerus lies the anatomical neck, and immediately below that lies the surgical neck, a common fracture site named because it is the neck a surgeon most often has to treat. Below the surgical neck sit the greater tuberosity laterally and the lesser tuberosity anteriorly, separated from each other by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, which carries the tendon of the long head of biceps brachii. This sequence, head, surgical neck, then the two tuberosities either side of the bicipital groove, is the humerus's own defining proximal landmark arrangement.

questions.title: The femur as the body's largest bone
questions.question: The femur is

options.A: The distal end of the femur formed of two femoral condyles (anterior and posterior)
options.B: Most of the shaft is smoothly rounded, except for a prominent ridge on its medial aspect (the linea aspera)
options.C: The femur is the longest and heaviest bone in the body
options.D: The lower end of the femur consists of a head, neck, and two trochanters

explanations.A: Incorrect. The femur's two distal condyles are named medial and lateral, not anterior and posterior.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The linea aspera is a posterior ridge on the femoral shaft, not one on its medial aspect.
explanations.C: Correct. The femur, the single long bone of the thigh, is the longest and heaviest bone in the human body, reflecting its role transmitting the full weight of the trunk from the hip joint to the knee joint. Its shaft is smoothly rounded except for the posterior linea aspera, and its lower end carries the two femoral condyles that articulate at the knee. Being built larger and heavier than any other bone is exactly what a weight-transmitting role of this kind requires.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The head, neck and two trochanters are landmarks of the femur's upper end, at the hip, not its lower end; the lower end instead carries the two femoral condyles.

questions.subject: msk
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Musculoskeletal System > Lower Limb Bones
questions.learning_objective: State that the femur is the longest and heaviest bone in the body.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: The femur is the longest and heaviest bone in the body" (QUIZ11&12 Q4).

questions.title: The fibula and the knee joint
questions.question: The fibula is

options.A: The lateral interosseous border gives attachment to the interosseous membrane
options.B: It takes no part in the articulation at the knee joint
options.C: The fibula is the slender medial bone of the leg
options.D: It takes a part in the transmission of body weight and provides attachment for muscles

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is the medial interosseous border of the fibula, not the lateral border, that gives attachment to the interosseous membrane joining it to the tibia.
explanations.B: Correct. The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the leg, and unlike the tibia it takes no part in the articulation at the knee joint; the knee joint is formed entirely between the femur and the tibia. The fibula bears very little of the body's weight, but it does provide attachment for muscles and contributes to the ankle joint distally, where its lower end forms the lateral malleolus. Its own articular contribution is therefore at the ankle, not the knee.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fibula is the slender lateral, not medial, bone of the leg; the tibia is the medial bone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The fibula takes very little part in transmitting body weight, which is carried mainly by the tibia; the fibula's main roles are muscle attachment and ankle-joint stability.

questions.title: Aspermia
questions.question: Aspermia means:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "No live sperms" within an otherwise present semen sample describes necrozoospermia, a different, narrower term from aspermia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "No sperms" within a present semen sample is azoospermia, not aspermia; aspermia is the absence of the semen itself.
explanations.C: Correct. Aspermia is the complete absence of semen, the whole ejaculate fluid, on ejaculation. It is distinct from azoospermia, the absence of live sperm within a semen sample that is otherwise present, and from asthenozoospermia, reduced sperm motility. Aspermia therefore describes a failure of ejaculation or semen production itself, not a defect confined to the sperm cells that would normally be carried within the semen.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "No motile sperms" describes asthenozoospermia, reduced sperm motility within a present semen sample, not the absence of semen itself.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: Define aspermia as the complete absence of semen, distinct from azoospermia and asthenozoospermia.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: no semen" (Quiz 31-32 Q6); stem recovered by rendering p203 after plain-text OCR left it blank on this section's own two-column layout.

questions.title: Spermatogenesis begins after puberty
questions.question: Spermatogenesi starts to occurs:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Marriage has no bearing on the biological onset of spermatogenesis, which is fixed by puberty, not by any social milestone.
explanations.B: Correct. In the male, gametogenesis (spermatogenesis) begins at puberty and continues without interruption into old age, so sperm are made afresh throughout adult life. This is the male schedule's own defining feature, and it stands in direct contrast to the female schedule, in which oogenesis instead begins in intrauterine life, is arrested, and resumes only at puberty.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Spermatogenesis does not begin in childhood; the testes remain reproductively immature until puberty.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Beginning in intrauterine life describes oogenesis, the female schedule; spermatogenesis in the male begins only at puberty.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that spermatogenesis begins at puberty and continues into old age, in contrast to oogenesis's own intrauterine start.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: after puberty" (Quiz 31-32 Q7); stem recovered by rendering p203.

questions.title: Spermatogenesis includes meiosis and spermiogenesis
questions.question: The process of spermatogenesis includes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Meiosis is a genuine part of spermatogenesis, but it is not the only part; naming meiosis alone leaves out spermiogenesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spermiogenesis is a genuine part of spermatogenesis, but it is not the only part; naming spermiogenesis alone leaves out meiosis.
explanations.C: Correct. Spermatogenesis, the whole process turning a spermatogonium into a mature spermatozoon, includes both meiosis, the two reduction divisions that turn a diploid primary spermatocyte into haploid spermatids, and spermiogenesis, the subsequent transformation of a round spermatid into a streamlined, motile spermatozoon without any further division. Because both processes are genuine, sequential parts of spermatogenesis as a whole, a question asking what the process includes is answered by naming both together.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Spermatocytosis" is not a recognised stage or process of spermatogenesis; it names no real step in the sequence.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: State that spermatogenesis as a whole includes both meiosis and spermiogenesis.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: all above" (Quiz 31-32 Q8); stem recovered by rendering p203.

questions.title: Sperm capacitation in the female genital tract
questions.question: Sperm is capable of fertilization after:

options.D: capacitation in the female genital tract

explanations.A: Incorrect. Merely being produced by the testis leaves sperm still incapable of fertilising an oocyte; further changes are required first.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Epididymal maturation gives sperm their forward motility, but it is not the final step that lets a sperm fertilise; capacitation, which happens later, is.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A specific process, capacitation, does answer this description, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.D: Correct. Capacitation is the removal of the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the sperm's surface over its acrosomal region, and it takes place specifically in the female genital tract. Only a capacitated sperm can bind zona pellucida receptors and undergo the acrosome reaction, releasing the enzymes needed to penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida, which is why capacitation in the female genital tract, not testicular production or epididymal maturation alone, is the step that confers fertilising capability.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that capacitation, occurring in the female genital tract, is the step that makes a sperm capable of fertilisation.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: capacitation in the female genital tract" (Quiz 31-32 Q9); stem recovered by rendering p203.

questions.title: FSH and testicular fluid production
questions.question: Follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) is essential for:

explanations.A: Correct. FSH acts mainly on the Sertoli cell of the seminiferous tubule, and two of its actions there are supporting the production of testicular (seminiferous tubule) fluid, the medium in which developing sperm are carried, and promoting the Sertoli cell's own synthesis of testosterone receptors, which is what lets the high local testosterone driven by LH actually act on spermatogenesis. Since both of these are genuine FSH actions on the Sertoli cell, the combined "all above" answer is the one that credits FSH with the full scope of what it does there.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Testicular fluid production is a genuine FSH action, but it is not the only one; testosterone-receptor synthesis is also credited to FSH.
explanations.C: Incorrect. FSH does have essential actions on the Sertoli cell, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Testosterone-receptor synthesis is a genuine FSH action, but it is not the only one; testicular fluid production is also credited to FSH.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: State that FSH supports both testicular fluid production and testosterone-receptor synthesis on the Sertoli cell.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: all above" (Quiz 31-32 Q10); stem recovered by rendering p203.

questions.title: The primary spermatocyte forms by mitosis
questions.question: Primary spermatocyte arise as a result of

explanations.A: Correct. The primary spermatocyte, the largest germ cell in the seminiferous epithelium, arises from a type B spermatogonium by an ordinary mitotic division, before that primary spermatocyte itself then undergoes the first meiotic (reduction) division to form two secondary spermatocytes. The mitotic step that produces the primary spermatocyte is what this question asks for, distinct from the meiotic divisions that follow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A specific mechanism, mitosis of the spermatogonium, does answer this description, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "First meiosis of spermatogonia" reverses the sequence: the spermatogonium itself divides by mitosis, not meiosis; it is the primary spermatocyte that later undergoes the first meiotic division.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The second meiotic division belongs to the secondary spermatocyte, forming spermatids, not to the spermatogonium forming the primary spermatocyte.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: State that the primary spermatocyte arises by mitosis of the spermatogonium, before its own meiotic division.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: simple mitosis of spermatogonia" (Quiz 31-32 Q11); this restatement is fully legible on p204 without needing a render, duplicating p202 Q1's own blank-stem printing of the same key.

questions.title: The spermatid's chromosome content
questions.question: Spermatid contains

explanations.A: Incorrect. "22-XY" would mean carrying both sex chromosomes at once, which does not happen; a haploid spermatid nucleus carries only one sex chromosome, either X or Y.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "44-XY" describes a diploid-range chromosome count, far more than the haploid content of a spermatid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "23-XY" again wrongly pairs both sex chromosomes together in one haploid nucleus, which does not occur.
explanations.D: Correct. Each gamete nucleus carries 22 autosomes and one sex chromosome. In the sperm, meiosis produces two kinds of spermatid in equal numbers: half carry 22 autosomes plus an X chromosome, half carry 22 autosomes plus a Y chromosome, which is exactly why the option is written as "22-X or 22-Y" rather than a single fixed formula. The ovum, by contrast, can only ever carry an X, which is why the sperm's own X-or-Y content is what determines the sex of the resulting child.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that a spermatid nucleus carries 22 autosomes and either an X or a Y chromosome.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: 22- X or 22 Y" (Quiz 31-32 Q12); fully legible on p204, duplicating p202 Q2's own blank-stem printing of the same key.

questions.title: The acrosomal cap forms from the Golgi apparatus
questions.question: In spermiogenesis, Golgi bodies give rise to

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mitochondrial sheath, which spirals around the sperm's middle piece, is built from the spermatid's own mitochondria, not from the Golgi apparatus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sperm's tail (flagellum) develops from one of the spermatid's centrioles, not from the Golgi apparatus.
explanations.C: Correct. During spermiogenesis, the Golgi apparatus of the spermatid packages hydrolytic enzymes into a vesicle that flattens over the nucleus to form the acrosomal cap, the structure that later releases acrosin and hyaluronidase to let the sperm penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida at fertilisation. This Golgi-to-acrosome pathway is the same rough-ER/Golgi packaging role the Golgi apparatus plays in other secretory cells, applied here to building the sperm's own penetrating enzyme cap.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The axial filament (axoneme) of the tail is built from microtubules organised by the centriole, not from the Golgi apparatus.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: State that the acrosomal cap forms from the spermatid's Golgi apparatus during spermiogenesis.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: acrosomal cap" (Quiz 31-32 Q13); fully legible on p204, duplicating p202 Q3's own blank-stem printing of the same key.

questions.title: Sperm viability window
questions.question: The average viable period of spermatozoa is about

explanations.A: Incorrect. One week overstates the sperm's own viable period; the window within which a sperm remains capable of fertilising an ovum is shorter.
explanations.B: Correct. Once formed, a mature spermatozoon remains viable and capable of fertilising an ovum for only about 3-4 days within the female genital tract. This short window, together with the ovum's own roughly similarly brief 1-2 day post-ovulatory lifespan, sets the practical fertile period around ovulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sixty-four days is roughly the duration of the whole process of spermatogenesis, not the sperm's own viable period after ejaculation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 120 days is the red blood cell's own lifespan, an unrelated figure, not the sperm's viable period.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: State that mature sperm remain viable for about 3-4 days.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: 3-4 days" (Quiz 31-32 Q14); fully legible on p204, duplicating p202's own blank-stem printing of the same key (there OCR'd as "3-4 days").

questions.title: Hormonal regulation of spermatogenesis
questions.question: Spermatogenesis is regulated by

explanations.A: Correct. Spermatogenesis is under combined pituitary hormonal control: luteinising hormone (LH) acts mainly on Leydig cells to drive testosterone production, and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) acts mainly on Sertoli cells, supporting testicular fluid production and testosterone-receptor synthesis there. Naming both FSH and LH together, rather than testosterone alone, is what correctly credits the process to its two pituitary regulators.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "All above" would have to include "testosterone" as a co-equal regulator alongside FSH and LH, but testosterone is itself the downstream product LH induces, not an independent pituitary regulator alongside it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Testosterone is essential for spermatogenesis but is the downstream hormone LH induces from Leydig cells, not itself one of the two pituitary regulators (FSH and LH) that this question asks for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Spermatogenesis does have identified hormonal regulators, FSH and LH, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: State that FSH and LH together regulate spermatogenesis.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: FSH and LH" (Quiz 31-32 Q15); fully legible on p204.

questions.title: Myosin is not a connective tissue fibre
questions.question: ....................is excluded as a proper connective tissue fiber

explanations.A: Correct. Connective tissue has three kinds of fibre: collagen, the commonest, with type I in dense connective tissue, type II in cartilage, type III as the reticular fibre and type IV in the basement membrane; reticular fibres, fine branching type III collagen; and elastic fibres, made of elastin with a fibrillin scaffold. Myosin is a contractile protein found in muscle cells, not a connective tissue fibre at all, so it is excluded from this three-fibre list entirely rather than being a fourth, less common type.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Elastic fibres are one of the three genuine connective tissue fibre types, not the excluded one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Collagen is one of the three genuine connective tissue fibre types, and the commonest of them, not the excluded one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reticular fibres are one of the three genuine connective tissue fibre types (fine type III collagen), not the excluded one.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Exclude myosin, a contractile muscle protein, from the three genuine connective tissue fibre types: collagen, elastic and reticular.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Myosin" (Quiz 33 Q1); stem recovered by rendering p205.

questions.title: Tendon as dense regular connective tissue
questions.question: Tendon is

explanations.A: Correct. A muscle may attach directly to bone or indirectly through a tendon, a cord of dense regular connective tissue, or an aponeurosis, a flattened sheet of the same tissue. "Regular" here means the collagen bundles run in parallel, all pulling in the one direction the tendon needs to transmit force from muscle to bone, which is exactly the mechanical demand a tendon has to meet.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dense irregular connective tissue has collagen bundles interwoven in different planes to resist pull from any direction, as in the dermis; a tendon's bundles instead run parallel, in one direction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mucoid connective tissue is a soft, hyaluronic-acid-rich jelly found in sites such as the umbilical cord, structurally unlike the tough parallel-bundled tendon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mesenchymal connective tissue is the embryonic precursor tissue from which other connective tissues develop, not the mature tissue of a formed tendon.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify tendon as dense regular connective tissue, its collagen bundles running parallel in one direction.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Dense regular connective tissue" (Quiz 33 Q2); stem recovered by rendering p205.

questions.title: Lamina propria as loose connective tissue
questions.question: lamina propria is

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mucoid connective tissue is the soft, hyaluronic-acid-rich jelly of sites such as the umbilical cord and vitreous humour, not the tissue of the lamina propria.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adipose connective tissue is fat-storing tissue; the lamina propria is not primarily a fat depot.
explanations.C: Correct. Loose areolar connective tissue is found everywhere in the body except the brain, including filling the spaces between organs, in the papillary layer of the dermis, in the lamina propria and submucosa of mucous membranes, in serous membranes, and around blood vessels and nerves. Because it is well vascularised and full of ground substance, the lamina propria's own loose connective tissue is exactly where nutrients and wastes are exchanged with the blood beneath the epithelium it supports.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mesenchymal connective tissue is the embryonic precursor tissue, not the mature loose connective tissue of the lamina propria.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the lamina propria's own connective tissue as loose (areolar) connective tissue.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Loose connective tissue" (Quiz 33 Q3); stem recovered by rendering p205.

questions.title: Orcein stains elastic fibres
questions.question: Elastic fibers stain dark brown with

explanations.A: Correct. The three connective tissue fibres are told apart by the stains that show them: collagen is pink with eosin, blue with Mallory's trichrome and red with van Gieson; elastic fibres are pink with eosin, brown with orcein and yellow with van Gieson; and reticular fibres are invisible in H&E, brown with silver and red with PAS. Orcein browns elastic fibres specifically, which is why it is the stain of choice when a slide needs to demonstrate elastic fibres on their own.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mallory's trichrome colours collagen blue; it does not brown elastic fibres.
explanations.C: Incorrect. PAS reacts with carbohydrate-rich structures such as reticular fibres and the basement membrane, colouring them red, not elastic fibres brown.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Routine H&E stains elastic fibres pink, indistinguishable from collagen; it does not brown them specifically.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that orcein stains elastic fibres brown, distinguishing them from collagen and reticular fibres.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Orcein stain" (Quiz 33 Q4); stem recovered by rendering p205.

questions.title: Hyaluronic acid as the main ground-substance GAG
questions.question: is the most common glycosaminoglycans in the ground substance of connective tissue

explanations.A: Correct. Connective tissue's ground substance is built mainly of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) together with proteoglycans and glycoproteins. Of the several GAGs present, hyaluronic acid is the most abundant, and it is also distinctive among them: a very large, non-sulfated GAG not covalently bound to a protein core, instead trapping enormous amounts of water to give ground substance its characteristic viscous, gel-like consistency. This combination of abundance and distinctive non-sulfated structure is what marks hyaluronic acid out from the other three options listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dermatan sulfate is a genuine GAG of ground substance, but a sulfated, protein-bound one, and less abundant than hyaluronic acid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Heparan sulphate is a genuine GAG, notably of basement membranes, but a sulfated, protein-bound one, and less abundant than hyaluronic acid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chondroitin sulfate is a genuine GAG, prominent in cartilage, but a sulfated, protein-bound one, and less abundant than hyaluronic acid.

questions.title: The fibroblast as a connective tissue cell
questions.question: Which of the following cells is a connective tissue cell

explanations.A: Correct. The fibroblast is the commonest cell of connective tissue proper, arising from undifferentiated mesenchymal cells and pericytes, and it exists in two states: the active fibroblast, branched with long processes and a protein-synthesising ultrastructure, and the resting fibrocyte, a smaller spindle cell. As a genuine connective-tissue-proper cell, the fibroblast is correctly grouped with connective tissue rather than with the epidermal cell types listed alongside it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A keratinocyte is the principal cell of the epidermis, an epithelial tissue, not a connective tissue cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A pericyte surrounds capillaries and can give rise to fibroblasts, but as a perivascular cell it is not itself classed among the connective-tissue-proper cell types this question is asking for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A Langerhans cell is an antigen-presenting dendritic cell resident in the epidermis, an epithelial tissue, not a connective tissue cell.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the fibroblast as a connective tissue cell, in contrast to epidermal cell types.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Fibroblast" (Quiz 34 Q1); stem recovered by rendering p207.

questions.title: Mast cells secrete histamine
questions.question: ..................... secrete histamine

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibroblasts secrete collagen, elastin, reticular fibres and ground substance; they do not secrete histamine.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Monocytes are phagocytic precursor cells of the mononuclear phagocyte system; histamine secretion is not their function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neutrophils are phagocytic granulocytes providing non-specific first-line defence; they do not secrete histamine.
explanations.D: Correct. The mast cell is a large, oval, fixed connective tissue cell whose cytoplasm is packed with metachromatic granules holding heparin, histamine and other mediators. On an appropriate stimulus, most often an IgE-mediated allergic trigger, the mast cell degranulates and releases its histamine, causing local vasodilatation and increased capillary permeability, the basis of an immediate hypersensitivity reaction. This histamine-secreting role is the mast cell's own defining function among the fixed cells of connective tissue.

questions.learning_objective: State that mast cells secrete histamine, the basis of an immediate hypersensitivity reaction.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Mast cells" (Quiz 34 Q2); stem recovered by rendering p207.

questions.title: Fibroblasts as the most common connective tissue cell
questions.question: ................. are the most common cell type of connective tissue

explanations.A: Correct. The fibroblast is the commonest cell of connective tissue proper, arising from undifferentiated mesenchymal cells and pericytes. Its active form is branched, with deeply basophilic cytoplasm and a large pale nucleus, well suited to its protein-synthesising job of laying down the fibres and ground substance that make up the bulk of connective tissue; this everyday synthetic role is exactly why it outnumbers the other, more specialised connective tissue cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mast cells are a resident but comparatively minor population, specialised for histamine release, not the most numerous connective tissue cell.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Macrophages are a wandering, phagocytic population, present but not the most numerous fixed cell of connective tissue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The mesenchymal cell is the undifferentiated precursor from which fibroblasts and other connective tissue cells arise; in mature connective tissue it is far outnumbered by the fibroblasts it has already given rise to.

questions.title: Adipocytes and the signet ring appearance
questions.question: -------------------- have signet ring appearance after staining with H&E under LM

explanations.A: Incorrect. Macrophages are identified by an irregular outline and a dark, kidney-shaped nucleus, not by a signet-ring appearance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mesenchymal cells are small, undifferentiated cells with scant cytoplasm; they do not show a signet-ring appearance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasma cells show an eccentric "clock-face" (cartwheel) nucleus with basophilic cytoplasm, a different appearance from the signet ring.
explanations.D: Correct. The unilocular (white) fat cell stores its fat as one large droplet containing dissolved lipid that displaces the cytoplasm and nucleus to the cell's periphery. Because the paraffin technique's xylol dissolves that droplet away, a routine H&E section shows the cell as an empty vacuole with a thin rim of cytoplasm and a flattened nucleus pressed against one side, the signet ring appearance -- the evidence that the cell held one large droplet rather than many small ones, and it is diagnostic of the unilocular adipocyte specifically.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the signet ring appearance on H&E as the diagnostic light-microscopic feature of the unilocular (white) fat cell.

questions.title: Basophils are the fewest circulating white blood cells
questions.question: The circulating white blood cells which are fewest in number are the

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neutrophils are the most numerous circulating white cell, about 60-70% of the total, the opposite of fewest.
explanations.B: Correct. Basophils make up only about 0-1% of the white cell count, the smallest proportion of any circulating leukocyte, reflecting how sparingly they normally circulate compared with the other granulocytes and lymphocytes. Their scarcity is exactly why finding an elevated basophil count (basophilia, above 2%) is itself a notable laboratory finding.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eosinophils, though a minority population, are more numerous than basophils.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Monocytes are more numerous than basophils, forming a larger minority of the circulating white cell count.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lymphocytes are the second most numerous circulating white cell after neutrophils, far more numerous than basophils.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that basophils are the fewest of the circulating white blood cells, about 0-1% of the total.

questions.title: The red blood cell's gas-transport function
questions.question: The function of the R.B.Cs. is:

options.D: Transport of oxygen to the tissues and CO2 to the lung

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phagocytosis is a white cell function, particularly of neutrophils and macrophages, not a function of the anucleate red corpuscle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A mature red corpuscle has no nucleus and cannot divide or reproduce itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secretion of formed products is not a red corpuscle function; it lacks the organelles (rER, Golgi) that secretion would require.
explanations.D: Correct. Every one of the red corpuscle's adaptations exists to serve gas transport: its flexible, selectively permeable membrane lets it squeeze through narrow capillaries while keeping haemoglobin in; its biconcave disc shape maximises surface area for gas exchange; and its lack of a nucleus and organelles frees its whole interior for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen to the tissues, while its carbonic anhydrase carries carbon dioxide back to the lung. This combination is what makes gas transport the red corpuscle's single defining function.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the red blood cell's function is transporting oxygen to the tissues and carbon dioxide to the lung.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Transport of oxygen to the tissues and CO2 to the lung" (Quiz 35 Q2); stem recovered by rendering p209.

questions.title: The neutrophil's multilobed nucleus
questions.question: The nucleus of neutrophils is

explanations.A: Incorrect. A rounded nucleus describes a lymphocyte, not a neutrophil.
explanations.B: Correct. The neutrophil carries a dark, segmented nucleus of two to five lobes joined by thin chromatin threads, alongside two granule populations: large, dark azurophil (primary) granules holding myeloperoxidase, and smaller, paler specific (secondary) granules holding collagenase, phagocytin, lysozyme and lactoferrin. This multilobed nucleus is the feature most often used to recognise the neutrophil on a blood film, and it is what gives the cell its alternative name, the polymorphonuclear leukocyte.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A kidney-shaped or indented nucleus describes a monocyte, not a neutrophil.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A bilobed nucleus describes an eosinophil, not a neutrophil, which characteristically has two to five lobes rather than a fixed two.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the neutrophil's nucleus is multilobed (two to five lobes), distinguishing it from other leukocytes.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Multilobed" (Quiz 35 Q3); stem recovered by rendering p209.

questions.title: The basophil's own function
questions.question: The main function of basophils is

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phagocytosis is the main function of neutrophils and macrophages, not basophils, which are not primarily phagocytic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pinocytosis, fluid-phase uptake, is not the basophil's defining function.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gas exchange is the red corpuscle's function, not the basophil's, which is a white cell with no role in carrying oxygen or carbon dioxide.
explanations.D: Correct. The basophil's specific granules hold histamine, heparin, eosinophil chemotactic factor and leukotrienes, and its cell membrane carries receptors for IgE. Heparin prevents clotting and promotes allergy, histamine causes vasodilatation with a sudden drop in blood pressure (anaphylaxis), and leukotrienes cause bronchospasm, so secreting heparin and histamine on degranulation is the basophil's own defining functional role among the circulating white cells.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the basophil's main function is secretion of heparin and histamine on degranulation.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Secretion of heparin and histamine" (Quiz 35 Q4); stem recovered by rendering p209.

questions.title: The red blood cell's biconcave profile
questions.question: The shape of the R.B.Cs from the side view is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A kidney shape describes the monocyte's nucleus, not the red corpuscle's own overall shape.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The red corpuscle has a precisely regular shape, not an irregular one; irregularity would defeat the uniform surface-area-to-volume ratio the cell depends on.
explanations.C: Correct. Seen from the side, the red corpuscle is a biconcave disc with rounded edges, thinner in the centre than at the rim. This shape gives a larger surface area for the cell's volume than a simple sphere would, letting the cell exchange gases more efficiently and flex easily through narrow or branched capillaries -- the side-view profile that complements its circular outline seen from above.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An oval shape describes certain other cells (such as an oval fat-cell nucleus), not the biconcave-disc profile of the red corpuscle.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the red blood cell is a biconcave disc when viewed from the side.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Biconcave" (Quiz 35 Q5); stem recovered by rendering p209.

questions.title: The red blood cell's circular outline from above
questions.question: The shape of the R.B.Cs from above is

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Biconcave" describes the red corpuscle's own side-view profile, not its outline seen from above.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Flat" does not capture the cell's own regular, circular outline from above; it is round, not simply flat.
explanations.C: Correct. Seen from above (en face), the red corpuscle presents a circular outline, complementing the biconcave profile seen from the side; together the two views describe a circular disc that is thinner in the centre than at its rim. This regular circular shape, combined with its flexible membrane, is what lets the cell pack efficiently and deform through narrow capillaries.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The red corpuscle's shape is precisely regular, not irregular; an irregular outline would work against the uniform surface area the cell relies on for gas exchange.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State that the red blood cell presents a circular outline when viewed from above, complementing its biconcave side profile.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Circular" (Quiz 35 Q6); fully legible on p210, no render needed.

questions.title: Oogenesis begins in intrauterine life
questions.question: The process of oogenesis starts...........................:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Beginning at puberty describes the male schedule, spermatogenesis; oogenesis begins far earlier, in intrauterine life.
explanations.B: Correct. In the female, oogenesis begins in intrauterine life -- the oocytes a woman will ever have are already present before she is born -- is then arrested, and resumes only at puberty, continuing through the ovarian cycles until the menopause. This intrauterine start is the female schedule's own defining feature, standing in direct contrast to the male schedule, which instead begins only at puberty and runs continuously thereafter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Early in childhood" is neither the start of oogenesis, which is intrauterine, nor its resumption, which is at puberty; oogenesis is arrested throughout childhood.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fertilisation is the trigger that lets the second meiotic division of an already-formed secondary oocyte complete; it is not when oogenesis as a whole starts.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that oogenesis begins in intrauterine life, in contrast to spermatogenesis's own start at puberty.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: early in the intrauterine life" (Quiz 36-37 Q1); stem recovered by rendering p211.

questions.title: Oogenesis is completed only after fertilization
questions.question: The process of oogenesis is completed..................:

explanations.A: Incorrect. At ovulation the oocyte is released but is still arrested at metaphase of the second meiotic division; ovulation alone does not complete oogenesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Soon before ovulation" is the timing of the first meiotic division's own completion (forming the secondary oocyte), not the timing of oogenesis's overall completion.
explanations.C: Correct. At ovulation the secondary oocyte has completed the first meiotic division but is arrested part-way through the second, at metaphase of meiosis II. This arrest is only released when a sperm penetrates the oocyte, the trigger that lets the second meiotic division complete, with extrusion of the second polar body -- so oogenesis as a whole is only completed after fertilisation, not before it or independently of it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A specific timing, after fertilisation, does answer this description, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that oogenesis is only completed after fertilisation, when the arrested oocyte's second meiotic division finishes.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: after fertilization" (Quiz 36-37 Q2); stem recovered by rendering p211.

questions.title: The primary oocyte's arrest until puberty
questions.question: primary oocyte starts dividing and reach the prophase of meiosis I. They remain as such (after birth) till............:

explanations.A: Correct. Oogenesis begins in intrauterine life, when primary oocytes enter and arrest in the prophase of the first meiotic division; this arrest persists all the way through childhood, after birth, and is only released when the ovarian cycles resume at puberty. Each ovarian cycle then carries one primary oocyte's own first meiotic division through to completion, forming a secondary oocyte, only from puberty onward.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A specific timing, the age of puberty, does answer this description, so "none of the above" is wrong.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fertilisation is the trigger that later releases the second meiotic division's own arrest, in the secondary oocyte, not the first meiotic division's arrest described here, which is released at puberty.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Birth itself does not release the arrest; the primary oocyte remains arrested in prophase of meiosis I from before birth all the way through childhood, until puberty.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that the primary oocyte remains arrested in prophase of meiosis I from before birth until puberty.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: the age of puberty" (Quiz 36-37 Q10, p213); fully legible without a render, duplicating p211 Q3's own blank-stem printing of the same key.

questions.title: Ovulation at the middle of the ovarian cycle
questions.question: Ovulation takes place at ...........:

options.A: at any time of the ovarian cycle
options.B: the end of the ovarian cycle (day 28)
options.C: the middle of the ovarian cycle (day 14)
options.D: the beginning of the ovarian cycle (day 1)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ovulation does not occur at any time in the cycle; it has a fixed timing around the cycle's midpoint, driven by the mid-cycle LH surge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Day 28, the end of a typical 28-day cycle, marks the onset of menstruation (the start of the next cycle), not ovulation.
explanations.C: Correct. Continuing the ovarian cycle's own timing, ovulation falls on the 14th day of a typical cycle, roughly its midpoint, once the mid-cycle LH surge (itself triggered by the dominant follicle's rising oestrogen) causes the mature follicle to rupture and release its secondary oocyte. This mid-cycle placement is what separates the preceding follicular phase from the following luteal phase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Day 1, the beginning of the cycle, marks the onset of menstruation, the start of the follicular phase, not ovulation.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that ovulation falls on day 14, the middle of a typical ovarian cycle.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: the middle of the ovarian cycle (day 14)" (Quiz 36-37 Q11, p213); fully legible without a render, duplicating p211 Q4's own blank-stem printing of the same key.

questions.title: The unfertilised ovum's short lifespan
questions.question: After the ovulation, the ovum lives for ................ after which it degenerates:

explanations.A: Correct. If fertilisation does not occur, the ovulated oocyte has no way to sustain itself indefinitely and degenerates about 1-2 days after ovulation. This short window, combined with the roughly similar few-day viability of sperm within the female genital tract, is what defines the narrow fertile period surrounding ovulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Six hours understates the ovum's own post-ovulatory lifespan, which extends to about 1-2 days.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Five to six days overstates the ovum's own post-ovulatory lifespan; it degenerates well before that if unfertilised.
explanations.D: Incorrect. One to two weeks greatly overstates the ovum's own post-ovulatory lifespan, which is measured in a day or two, not weeks.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that an unfertilised ovum degenerates about 1-2 days after ovulation.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: 1-2 days" (Quiz 36-37 Q12, p213); fully legible without a render, duplicating p211 Q5's own blank-stem printing of the same key.

questions.title: The corpus luteum's lifespan without fertilisation
questions.question: If the ovum is not fertilized corpus luteum persists for about ..... :

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sixteen days overstates the corpus luteum of menstruation's own fixed lifespan.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eighteen days overstates the corpus luteum of menstruation's own fixed lifespan.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ten days understates the corpus luteum of menstruation's own fixed lifespan.
explanations.D: Correct. If fertilisation does not occur, the corpus luteum of menstruation has a fixed functional lifespan of about 12-14 days from ovulation, after which it regresses into the fibrous corpus albicans, and its falling progesterone output is what triggers endometrial shedding. If implantation does occur instead, hCG from the syncytiotrophoblast rescues the corpus luteum from this regression, and the resulting corpus luteum of pregnancy instead persists for about 3-4 months, with the placenta then taking over progesterone production.

questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Female Reproductive System > Ovarian Cycle
questions.learning_objective: State that the corpus luteum of menstruation persists about 12-14 days if fertilisation does not occur.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: 14 days" (Quiz 36-37 Q6); stem recovered by rendering p212.

questions.title: The LH surge triggers ovulation
questions.question: Ovulation occurs under the effect of ...............:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Progesterone dominates the luteal phase that follows ovulation; it is not the hormone that triggers ovulation itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rising oestrogen from the dominant follicle is what triggers the LH surge, but it is the LH surge itself, not oestrogen directly, that triggers ovulation.
explanations.C: Correct. The ovarian cycle's follicular phase is driven by pituitary FSH, which matures a dominant follicle; the rising oestrogen that follicle produces then triggers a sharp mid-cycle surge in luteinising hormone (LH). It is this LH surge that is the immediate trigger for ovulation, the rupture of the mature follicle and release of the secondary oocyte, and it is also what converts the ruptured follicle into the corpus luteum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. FSH drives the earlier follicular-growth phase, maturing the dominant follicle; it is the later LH surge, not FSH, that triggers ovulation itself.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.module_subject: AUN-PMS-102 > Female Reproductive System > Ovarian Cycle
questions.learning_objective: State that a surge in luteinising hormone (LH) is the immediate trigger for ovulation.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: LH" (Quiz 36-37 Q7); stem recovered by rendering p212.

questions.title: Fertilization occurs in the ampulla of the oviduct
questions.question: Fertilization normally takes place in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cervical canal is the passage the sperm swims through en route to the uterus; it is not the site where fertilisation occurs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The peritoneal cavity is not a normal fertilisation site; an oocyte fertilised there would represent a rare, abnormal (primary abdominal) ectopic pregnancy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By the time a fertilised conceptus reaches the uterine cavity it has already progressed to the morula stage, several days after fertilisation, so fertilisation itself does not occur there.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The isthmus is the narrower, medial part of the uterine tube nearer the uterus; fertilisation occurs more laterally, in the ampulla.
explanations.E: Correct. The normal site of fertilisation is the ampulla, the lateral (wide) part of the uterine tube, where the ovulated secondary oocyte meets capacitated sperm. Fertilisation does not normally occur in the uterine cavity, the isthmus, the peritoneal cavity or the cervical canal; by the time the conceptus reaches the uterine cavity it has already progressed to the morula stage, several days after fertilisation took place in the ampulla.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla (lateral part) of the uterine tube.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: Ampulla of oviduct" (Quiz 38-41 Q1); stem recovered by rendering p214.

questions.title: The fertilized ovum's transit to the uterine cavity
questions.question: In how many days after fertilization does the fertilized ovum enter the uterine cavity

explanations.A: Incorrect. One day is too short; the conceptus is still undergoing early cleavage stages within the uterine tube at this point, not yet in the uterine cavity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eight days overstates the transit time; a conceptus that has not yet reached the uterine cavity by then would be unusually delayed.
explanations.C: Correct. The zygote, and the 2-cell, 4-cell and other early cleavage stages that follow it, all occur within the uterine tube. The morula is the first stage of the conceptus to complete this tubal journey and reach the uterine lumen, doing so about 3-4 days after fertilisation -- a window sometimes quoted as a fixed "day 4" but better understood as 3-4 days, since transport time varies somewhat.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fourteen days is far too long for tubal transit; it instead corresponds roughly to implantation-era events, well after the conceptus has already reached and left the uterine cavity's early stages.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Seven days overstates ordinary tubal transit time to the uterine cavity, though it is closer to when implantation itself begins after the conceptus has already arrived there.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that the morula, the first stage to complete tubal transit, reaches the uterine cavity about 3-4 days after fertilisation.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: 3 days" (Quiz 38-41 Q2); stem recovered by rendering p214.

questions.title: Pronuclei fuse at fertilization
questions.question: Haploid nuclei that fuse at fertilization are called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mitotic figures are the visible chromosome arrangements of a dividing cell during mitosis, not the haploid nuclei of the gametes at fertilisation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Centrioles are small cytoplasmic structures that organise microtubules and the mitotic spindle; they are not nuclei at all.
explanations.C: Correct. Immediately after a sperm penetrates the oocyte, each gamete's own haploid nucleus is called a pronucleus. The male and female pronuclei then move together and fuse, restoring the diploid chromosome number and completing fertilisation -- the naming of these two haploid nuclei as "pronuclei", specifically in the brief interval before they fuse, is what this question tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Homunculi" is an obsolete, disproven historical idea (a miniature preformed human supposedly inside the sperm), not a real structure or the name for the fusing gamete nuclei.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: Name the pronuclei as the haploid gamete nuclei that fuse at fertilisation, restoring the diploid number.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: pronuclei" (Quiz 40 Q1); fully legible on p217, no render needed; duplicates Quiz 38-41 Q4's own blank-stem printing of the same key (p214).

questions.title: Capacitation is essential for fertilization
questions.question: Capacitation of the sperm

options.C: is caused by the zona pellucid

explanations.A: Incorrect. Preventing polyspermy is the job of the zona reaction after the first sperm fuses with the oocyte, a separate mechanism from capacitation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Capacitation occurs in the female genital tract, not in the male; it is the removal of the sperm's surface coat that happens only after ejaculation, within the female tract.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Capacitation is not caused by the zona pellucida; it happens in the female genital tract before the sperm ever reaches the zona, and it is what then lets the sperm bind zona pellucida receptors.
explanations.D: Correct. Capacitation is the removal of the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the sperm's surface over its acrosomal region, occurring in the female genital tract. Only a capacitated sperm can bind zona pellucida receptors and undergo the acrosome reaction, releasing the enzymes needed to penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida, which is exactly why capacitation is essential for fertilisation to occur at all.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that capacitation, occurring in the female genital tract, is essential for fertilisation.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: is essential for fertilization" (Quiz 40 Q2); fully legible on p217, no render needed; duplicates Quiz 38-41 Q5's own blank-stem printing of the same key (p214).

questions.title: Early cleavage increases cell number, not size
questions.question: The early stages of cleavage are characterized by

options.A: increase in the size of the cells in the zygote
options.B: increase in the number of cells in the zygote
options.C: formation of a hollow ball of cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cleavage does not increase the size of the individual cells; each division instead produces smaller cells (blastomeres) from the fixed volume of zygote cytoplasm.
explanations.B: Correct. Cleavage is a rapid series of mitotic divisions of the zygote, defined specifically as an increase in the number of cells (blastomeres) making up the conceptus, not by any growth in its overall size. Each division simply repackages the same fixed volume of zygote cytoplasm into more, smaller cells, which is why the early cleavage stages do not enlarge as they divide; true growth only begins later, after implantation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Formation of a hollow ball of cells describes the later blastocyst stage, not the earliest cleavage stages.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The zona pellucida is already present from the primary oocyte stage onward, before cleavage begins; cleavage does not form it.

questions.subject: dev
questions.learning_objective: State that early cleavage is defined by an increase in the number of cells in the zygote, not by growth in size.

field_notes.keySource: Moodle attempt-review, "The correct answer is: increase in the number of cells in the zygote" (Quiz 40 Q3); fully legible on p217, no render needed; duplicates Quiz 38-41 Q6's own blank-stem printing of the same key (p215).

questions.title: The zona pellucida through the early blastocyst
questions.question: With the light microscope, the zona pellucida appears as a translucent membrane surrounding the:

options.E: all of the above are correct

explanations.A: Incorrect. The zona pellucida does surround the primary oocyte, but it also surrounds every later stage listed, so "primary oocyte" alone is an incomplete answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The zona pellucida does surround the zygote, but it also surrounds the other stages listed, so "zygote" alone is an incomplete answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The zona pellucida does surround the morula, but it also surrounds the other stages listed, so "morula" alone is an incomplete answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The zona pellucida does surround the very early blastocyst, but it also surrounds the earlier stages listed, so this alone is an incomplete answer.
explanations.E: Correct. The zona pellucida is present from the primary oocyte stage onward and continues to surround the zygote and every cleavage stage -- morula and early blastocyst alike -- keeping the conceptus at a constant overall size and preventing premature adhesion to the tubal wall. It does not persist all the way to implantation: the blastocyst must first "hatch," shedding the zona pellucida, before its trophoblast can attach directly to the endometrium, so the zona is gone before implantation, not after it.

questions.title: Cleavage begins in the oviduct
questions.question: In humans, cleavage begins in the

explanations.A: Incorrect. By the time the conceptus reaches the uterus it has already progressed to the morula stage, several days into cleavage, not at its start.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ovulation, the release of the oocyte, occurs at the ovary, but fertilisation and the first cleavage divisions occur later, in the oviduct (uterine tube), not in the ovary itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The normal site of fertilisation is the ampulla, the lateral part of the uterine tube (oviduct), where the ovulated oocyte meets capacitated sperm; cleavage, the fertilised zygote's earliest divisions, begins at that same tubal site immediately afterward. The zygote and its earliest cleavage stages -- 2-cell, 4-cell and beyond -- all occur within the uterine tube as the conceptus is carried toward the uterine cavity, which it does not reach until the later morula stage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vagina is the copulatory canal through which sperm are deposited; fertilisation and cleavage take place much further along the tract, in the oviduct.

questions.title: Granulosa cells as the corpus luteum's progesterone source
questions.question: Granulosa cells are the primary source of

explanations.A: Incorrect. FSH is a pituitary gonadotropin, not a product of the granulosa cell itself.
explanations.B: Correct. Within the ovarian follicle and, after ovulation, within the corpus luteum, thecal cells mainly supply androgen precursors while granulosa cells convert those precursors to oestrogen during the follicular phase and, after luteinisation, become the main source of progesterone during the luteal phase. It is specifically the granulosa cells, once luteinised, that are credited as the corpus luteum's principal progesterone-secreting population, not the thecal cells acting alone or jointly with them.
explanations.C: Incorrect. LH is a pituitary gonadotropin, not a product of the granulosa cell itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Oestrogen is the granulosa cell's own product during the earlier follicular phase, before luteinisation; after luteinisation its main secretory product becomes progesterone.
